This has the intended effect, and the

ing came the little girl did not awake

$50 away, dog!"

The beauteous robe she wore;
Its folds golden belt embraced,
One rose-hued gem it bore.
The girdle shrank its lessening round
Still kept the shining gem,
But now her flowing locks it bound,
A lustrous diadem.

Behold! glittering band,
Its ruseate diamond set anew,


Her neck's white column spanned.
Suns rise and set; the straining clasp
The shortened links resist,
Yet flashes in bracelets grasp
The diamond on her wrist.
At length, the round of changes past,
The thieving years could bring,
The jewel, glittering to the last,
Still sparkles in ring.
So, link by link, our friendships part,
So loosen, break and fall,
A narrowing zone; the loving heart
Lives changeless through them all.

Sweet friend, when thou and are gone
Beyond earth's weary labor,
When small shall be our need of grace
From comrade or from neighbor,
Passed all the strife, the toll, the care
And done with all the signing,
What tender truth shall we have gained,
Alas, by simple dying?
Then lips too chary of their praise
Will tell our merits over,
And eyes too swift our faults to see
Shall no defect discover.
Then hands that would not lift stone
Where stones were thick to cumber
Our steep-hill path, will scatter flowers
Above our pillowed slumber.
Sweet friend, perchance both thou and +,
Ere love is past forgiving,
Should take the earnest lesson home
Be patient with the living.
To-day's repressed rebuke may save
Our binding tears tomorrow
Then patience-e'en when keenest edge
May whet q nameless sorrow.
'Tis easy to be gentle when


Deaths silence shames our clamor,
And easy to discern the best


Through memory's mystic glamour; ,
But wise it were for thee and me, IS
Ere love is past forgiving,
To take the tender lesson home
Be patient with the living.

Farewell, Old Year, farewell to you;


You've been for many day,
A friend most tried, friend most true
And as we bid you our adieu,
We give our heartfelt thanks to 70


And speed you on your way.
We've had full many merry time,


Since first we met, Old Year.
You've sung for us the Christmas rhyme,
And rung for us the Christmas chime,
And many joy at Christmas time


You brought with hearty cheer.
You crowned the woodland banks with bloom
Of roses red and sweet
s You gave the violets their perfume,
Ripened the cornfeId's tasseled plume,
And filled the mill wheels running fume,
To grind the golden wheat.
You brought the yellow daffodil


To blossom in the spring
Strewed cuckoo flowers on every hill,
And cat-tails by the ripping rill-
And taught the lonely whip-poor-will
His vesper song to sing.
You turned the ivy's green to red,


The maple leaves to gold
--PurpIed the clusters overhead,
And showers of ripened nuts you shed,
When fallen leaves lay thickly spread
Abo re the forest mold.
And if you gathered some fair flowers
That blossomed on your way,
You bore them to o fairer clime,
Where neither cold, nor care, nor Time
Could blight them in their golden prime,
Or touch them with decay.
And ali! you brought, Old Year! Old Year!
One tiny baby flower
To nestle ON its mothers breast,
And close its blue eyes into rest,
When song birds seek their cradle nest
At twilight's shadowy hour.
And now, Old Year, farewell to you
We grieve to lose you So
You've been friend both tried and true,
And as we bid you our adieu,
We give heartfelt thanks to you,


And sigh that you must go.


Helen Whitney Clark.

prietors Of the Canada Rancho, has
been clearing brush, moving rocks,

almightiness to the mind, was not

which was played upon her can be left
to the imagination. The contrast be-
tween a wretched cabin of boards, with
one room, broken stove and that dis
NAL rusty tin cup, and an elegant resi-
dence with large and spacious rooms

certainly strong aud sweet surprise.

Nervous, enthusiastic and talkative
women are the foam and sparkle; quiet
women the wine of life. The senses
ache and grow weary of the perpetual
glare and brilliancy of the former, but
turn with a sense of security and re-
pose to the mild, mellow glow irradia-
ting the sphere of the latter.


We associate all ideas of rest with
quiet women. They are the soul divin-
tiles reverently guarding their sacred
trusts in the Court of Silence. The
quiet woman moves in an atmosphere
ofbenignant grace. Appealing, strong,
compelling, her pure life is petition or
prayer. When she speaks, her words
are aptly chosen and fifty spoken. She
is wise and thoughtful, but loving and
meek. "Still waters run deep" but
not in the worldly applied sense; bab-
bling rills do not wear their channels
deep, but streams of calmest flow have
hidden depths undreamed of, uDsus-
pected.


The touch of a quiet woman's hand





magic, all the precious memories which
time has blotted from life's calendar of
years, and restores the beautiful lost
visions of childhood, when the rainbow
of mothers smiles spanned the rosy
horizon, and the young heart thrilled
the music of her lullaby as she rocked
us in dreams upon her pure bosom.


We confde in the quiet woman.
Truth encircles them as with halo,
and they give us constancy in return
for our faith. In sorrow, adversely, i'll
ness, the quiet woman isnurse, counsel
or and friend. She soothes, comforts
and caresses, and is the unfaltering
guide of the weak and unerring in
stincts. Into her steady and skillful
hands the physician trusts the spark,
we'll knowing that the faithful sentinel
will not tire in her watch, nor sleep
upon her post. She moves silently and
orderly; even her light garments falling
in soft, harmonious flow. She does not
irritate with questions, but surprises and
pleases by her unobtrusiveness and an
ticipations. She rarely speaks, but
when she does her tones are firm and
sweet and low, and linger upon the sick
and drowsy ear like the musical vibration
of murmuring waves. No other step
approaches so breezy and life-giving.
Such glory ofrepose surround her, and
her kisses, rarely bestowed, are like
benedictions. The love ofQuiet women

! Accident on the Maryland Central.-The
rear of the morning train from Delta to Balti-
more, on the Maryland Central Railroad, on Mon
| day last, jumped the track at a curve near the
overshot treste, south of Faston, and was dragged
for distance on the cross ties, and then up
setting broke from the train and rolled down an
embankment, landing on its side, with the wheels
upwards. There were about 80 passengers inside,
including five ladies. All the passengers were
severely jolted, and were tumbled together in a
mass when the turned over. The train was
stopped within a short distance and the rear door
of the wrecked car was broken open and the peo-
pie inside extricated. A physician, who was in
another car, promptly on hand to dress the
wounds of the injured. Thomas Brooks, of Con-
stitution, York county, had his head badly cut;
David Brebeg, of Hartford county, had his hip
hurt, and Wilson West, from near Belair, had his
nose broken. One of the ladies had bruised
arm, and the other passengers sustained slight
casualties. The car took fire from the upset
stove, but this was extinguished without trouble.
The ground where the jumped down the
bankment was wet and spongy and stopped it
from rolling over to the bottom. The glass in the
car windows was smashed, and the side of the
and one of the trucks were broken. The passen-
gers, who made such a narrow escape, were taken
on board the train, which started for Baltimore,
but was again stopped by the breaking of the
couplings of another passenger coach. Ropes
were utilized to repair the break. 1t is thought
the accident was caused by the spreading of the
tracks, which had become unsettled by the wet
weather. Col. L. H. Webster was one of the pas
sengers who was tumbled down the embankment.

scene at the Star Theatre caused by the cry

The performance had proceeded without

and the whole audience instantly rose to

mass of panic stricken and struggling hui

Few Of those wearing sealskin sacque have
any knowledge of the process by which the skins
are prepared for use Seen when first taken from
the animal they little resemble the warm, glossy
skins worn upon our streets, for until dyed and
cured they are of a light brown hue, coarse and
full of sand Before becoming valuable they are
shaved down on the flesh side until not thicker
than paper, the long hairs are pulled out and the
fur dyed. The cost of the article is due to the
labor expended on it. The raw skins sold in
London, where the finishing is done, and then
shipped back to America, where they are sold
with heavy duty added. The killing season in
Alaska begins about the 18th of June, and the
100, 900 skins are usually ready for shipment n
month later. The work of slaughtering the ami
mails is done by natives who live upon the st.
Paul and St. George Islands and the process is an
interesting one. When skins are wanted the ma
tives go to the rookeries station themselves along
the shore between the seals and the water, and,
at given signal, spring to their feet and make
as much noise as possible. The frightened vic
tins, timid as deer, then stampede up the beach
and are driven like sheep few miles inland, until
their captors attack them with hickory clubs.
Being knocked senseless, they are stabbed with
long, sharp knives and the skins are quickly
stripped from the bodies. The work is divided
among the men-some knocking the seals down,
others stabbing them and still others taking off
the skins. The native Indians number about
800, and under the terms of the lease, are pro-
vided by the company with warm houses, sixty
tons of coal, doctor and a schoolmaster salmon
and other necessities and comforts. For their
labor the men are paid some $4,000 altogether
each season, a sum more than sufficient to meet
the limited needs of life in region of almost
perpetual fogs and utter isolation.

Charles Dickens, when he first visited Wash
ington in 1912, was just entering his thirtieth
year. He was middle-sized somewhat fieshy
person. and he wore a brown frOck coat, a red
figured vest and fancy scarf cravat that con-
cealed the collar and was fastened to the bosom
in rather voluptuOus folds by double pin and
chain His hair, which was long and dark,
grew low upon the brow, had a wavy kink where
1t started from the head. and was corkscrewed
as it fell on either side of his face. His fore
head retreated gradually from the eyes. without
any marked protuberance save at the outer
angle, the upper portion of which formed
prominent ridge little within the assigned po-
sition of the organ of idealty. The eyebas
completely filled their sockets. The aperture
monty clear or bright, but quick, moist and ex-
pressive. The nose was slightly aquiline, the
mouth of moderate dimensions making no great
display of the teeth. the facial muscles OCCASION
ally drawing the upper lip most strongly on the
left side as the mouth opened in speaking. His
features, taken together, were well proportioned,
of glowing and cordial aspect with more ami
nation than grace and more intelligence than
beauty.

Last week the cable brought glowing pic
ture from the heart of Africa. One unarmed Eng
lshman, who had trayersed without guard
thousand miles of desert beset with foes, drew


near city where weak Egyptian garrison trem-


bled at vague rumors of the approach OF many
thousand savage warriors. "The natives went

And he answered, come without soldiers, Cod

"wll not fight with any weapon but justice.
aThere shall be no moro BazOuks." "lhen
Gordon publicly burned at Khartoum the tax


"bOoks, the whips and the whipping posts"
At his word Central Africa is revolutionized.
Cairo telegraphs to London: The influence OF
Gordon with the Arabs rs so great that
sKhartoum is now safe without troops" The
rescue that all England could not have given In
time was brought by one man armed with
Justice only. Before him, Egyptian greed and
oppression, and Moslem fanaticism, alike
shrink back. "The Arabs say" dispatch
reads, that Gordon gives them more than FL
Mahdi could offer" These are savages. But
even with them, one man who speaks truth, and
docs Justice, and breaches Christianity In his
acts, proves more powerful than all armies.


This century has not presented grander
sight. The lofty courage of the man, and his
sublime reliance upon simple justice and his
own proved character to sway the acts OF
multitudcs-how they contrast with the bonn
bardment of Alexandria When has there been
q finer exhibition of moral pOwerP -Four years
had elapsed since he had been in Central Africa.
When he started, England trembled for his
life; "thc natives would probably have
forgotten him." No. Justice is so rare thing
that Africa does not forget it. This man had
once ruled in the Soudan with such wisdom and
such goodness that his word has power. There
shall be no more BazoukS." The day OF the
hreIings and plunderers, who rob once Tor the
Khedivo and twice for themselves, is over
Only one man had the power to make England
comprehend that this was the thing necessary
in the Soudan. Happily for her own honor
England had sent that man to make justice
supreme, and, though the right thing was
tardily done, it was done at last.


Had Gordon and Justice gone earlier to the
Nile, brave men need not have died. 1t must
remain a reproach to the British Government
that it did not take. months ago, the one step
that was necessary to restore peace III the
Soudan. Greed and cruelty, plumber and
crime, have been tolerated too long under the
shelter of the British flag. For it has been true
ever since Arab first revolted that England
has been responsible for what happened in
Egypt and in tho SOudan. The responsibility
is now acknowledged; and Christian nations
may well rejoice that England at last honors
the Christian faith by sending truth and justice
to the Moslem world.
